hints: Start with what you can see clearly - which cell has a large intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes, and which cell already shows a new cell plate forming between two daughter nuclei? Those must be the start and the end.
walkthrough:
Anchor the Start and End**
You are sitting with Fig. 6.1. Cell A shows a large grey interphase nucleus with nucleolus and no condensed chromosomes. That is the cell before mitosis starts. Cell F shows two separate daughter nuclei with a cell plate forming down the middle. That is cytokinesis, the very end.

Order the Middle by Chromosome Behaviour**
After A, chromatin condenses into long tangled threads in C (early prophase). Then chromosomes get shorter, thicker and line up in the middle in E (metaphase). Then sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles in D (anaphase). Then two new nuclear envelopes reform around decondensing chromosomes in B (telophase), before cytokinesis in F. So the full order is A - C - E - D - B - F.
Final answer: 1 A, 2 C, 3 E, 4 D, 5 B, 6 F

walkthrough:
DNA Replication Happens Before Mitosis Is Visible**
In interphase, specifically S phase, the cell replicates its DNA so each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids. No condensed chromosomes are visible yet, which is why cell A looks uniform grey.

Condensation Prepares Chromosomes for Movement**
In prophase, chromatin supercoils and condenses into short, thick, visible chromosomes, as seen in cell C. The nuclear envelope also breaks down.

Centromere Division Triggers Separation**
In anaphase, the centromeres holding sister chromatids together divide. This allows sister chromatids to become separate daughter chromosomes, as seen pulling apart in cell D.

Spindle Contraction Moves Chromosomes**
Also in anaphase, spindle fibres attached to centromeres contract and shorten, pulling daughter chromosomes to opposite poles. Metaphase just before this is when chromosomes are organised at the equator, as in cell E.
Final answer: DNA replication - interphase (S phase); division of centromeres - anaphase; condensation of chromatin - prophase; contraction of spindle fibres - anaphase.

hints: Think about the numbers problem in immunity - only one or a few lymphocytes recognise a specific antigen, so what type of cell division is needed to quickly make thousands of copies?
Recall what the different clones become - which B-cell derivative makes antibody, and which T-cells help or kill?
Think beyond the immediate infection - what identical cells are left behind to give a faster secondary response?
walkthrough:
One Cell Is Not Enough - Make a Clone**
When a B or T lymphocyte with a specific receptor binds its antigen, it is activated. It then divides repeatedly by mitosis in clonal expansion. Because mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells, the whole clone keeps the same specificity.

Build an Army of Effector Cells**
The clone provides numbers fast. Many B-cell clones differentiate into plasma cells that secrete large amounts of specific antibody. Many T-helper cell clones secrete cytokines to stimulate B cells, macrophages and T-cytotoxic cells. Many T-cytotoxic cell clones kill infected body cells directly.

Leave Memory for Next Time**
Some cells of the clone become long-lived memory B and memory T cells. They remain in circulation so a second exposure to the same antigen gives a faster, stronger secondary immune response.

Final answer: Mitosis gives clonal expansion to produce large clones of genetically identical lymphocytes specific to the antigen; many B cells differentiate into plasma cells to make antibody; many T-helper cells to stimulate other cells and many T-cytotoxic cells to kill infected cells; memory B and T cells produced for secondary response.
